<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices is increasingly important to enhance on-device intelligence.
Weight quantization is crucial for reducing the memory footprint of LLMs on devices.
However, low-bit LLMs necessitate <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">mixed precision matrix multiplication (mpGEMM)</span> of low precision weights and high precision activations during inference.
Existing systems, lacking native support for mpGEMM, resort to dequantize weights for high precision computation.
Such an indirect way can lead to a significant inference overhead.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce T-MAC, an innovative lookup table(LUT)-based method designed for efficient low-bit LLM (i.e., weight-quantized LLM) inference on CPUs.
T-MAC directly supports mpGEMM without dequantization, while simultaneously eliminating multiplications and reducing additions required.
Specifically, T-MAC transforms the traditional data-type-centric multiplication to bit-wise table lookup, and enables a unified and scalable mpGEMM solution.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">Our LUT-based kernels scale linearly to the weight bit-width. Evaluated on low-bit Llama and BitNet models, T-MAC demonstrates up to 4<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> increase in throughput and 70% reduction in energy consumption compared to <span id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span>. For BitNet-b1.58-3B, T-MAC delivers a token generation throughput of 30 tokens/s with a single core and 71 tokens/s with eight cores on M2-Ultra, and 11 tokens/s on Raspberry Pi 5. T-MAC with LUT-based computing paradigm, paves the way for the practical deployment of low-bit LLMs on resource-constrained edge devices without compromising computational efficiency. The system is open-sourced at <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/T-MAC" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/T-MAC</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Large Language Models, General Matrix Multiplication, Low-bit Quantization, Computing Algorithms
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">More and more large language models (LLMs) are deploying on client devices, such as smartphones, desktops, and robotics, to provide unprecedented intelligence services, real-time task response and user data protection. Typical examples are Phi-3-mini-4bit deployed on iPhone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>)</cite>, Llama-2-7B-4bit on Pixel 5 and Llama-2-13B-4bit on Apple M2 Ultra <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>)</cite>, as well as the recent Microsoft Copilot+PC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite> that collaboratively run the on-device LLM with the on-cloud LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Low-bit weight quantization is a must-have for on-device LLM inference due to the hardware resource limitation. LLM inference quality is also robust to precision loss. Beyond 4-bit, 3-bit, 2-bit and even 1-bit models are emerging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>)</cite>. By comparison, activation quantization cannot follow the trend due to outliers. The computing operands thus have asymmetric precision and bit width, such as W4A16, W2A16, or W1A8<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          W# means the bit-width of weight and A# means the bit-width of activation</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, current commodity hardware still supports fixed bit-width and symmetric operands, and cannot support these various and mixed precision. Even some research papers support asymmetric bit-width operands. The bit-width is still fixed, such as W4A8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>)</cite>. Computing kernels have to convert/dequantize low-bit weight to match the activation, and compute on hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This conversion raises two obvious issues. <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> Performance wise, the conversion cost offsets the gain from bit scaling down. Our evaluation (ref Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.1. Evaluation Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) shows that scaling down bits from 4 bit to 1 bit even increases latency cost for most of the cases. <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> Development wise, the data layout and kernels need to be designed case by case for each mixed precision. For example, the data layouts, as well as the interleaving or swizzling methods for W3 and W2 are totally different. The kernels need to be redesigned to match the layout.
Therefore, to deploy LLM on devices, a fundamental problem is how to directly and efficiently support mpGEMM (mixed precision General Matrix Multiplication) of low bit weights and high bit activations on devices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This paper aims a mpGEMM kernel design, which is independent of hardware data types and the bit width of the quantization algorithms, to achieve scalable speedup with bit scaling down. To realize that, our <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">key concept</span> is that rather than the dominant data-type-centric calculation, we exploit the <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bit-wise</span> calculation of the standard algorithm of multiplication. That is, the multiplication of two numbers can be transformed into multiplying one number by each bit of the other number, then shifting and adding the partial products. The mpGEMM between activation and weight matrices is decomposed into a series (= the bit-width of weight) of mpGEMM between activation and a one-bit matrix, and then adds the partial results up. This method can thus support any bit-width combination of activation and weight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A promising method to implement bit-wise calculation is by table lookups <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite>. Since one bit can only represent two values, e.g., 1/-1, the bit patterns of a one-bit vector are limited. For example, if a one-bit matrix is partitioned into groups of four-element vector, the number of possible bit patterns (e.g., [1,1,1,-1] and [1,1,-1,-1]) for each group is only <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given an activation, it can be first computed with all possible bit patterns and saved in tables. The mpGEMM of activation and one-bit matrix is then transformed to table lookup indexed by each bit pattern in weight, and addition to accumulate the looked-up results. The mpGEMM is reduced to table lookup+add operations and no multiplication.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Though bit-wise LUT-based mpGEMM could reduce multiplications, how to efficiently implement it on real devices is challenging, since current hardware is highly tailored to multiplication. The <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">outstanding difference</span> between bit-wise LUT and traditional mpGEMM is the two operands for LUT method are tables and index matrices, rather than activation and weight. The data format and layout of the two operands are thus critical to the inference speed. <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> One challenge is that compared to the continuous data access for activation and weight, the access to tables are random. The residence of tables in fast on-chip memory will be particularly important for final inference performance. <span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> However, the on-chip memory is limited, and the LUT method enlarges the on-chip memory usage compared to traditional mpGEMM. This is because the LUT needs to save the results of the activation vector multiplied with all possible bit patterns. This is exponentially more than the activation itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">By solving the challenges, this paper proposes T-MAC mpGEMM kernel library. As shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, it is based on the concept of bit-wise calculation and LUT implementation, and provide unified and scalable solution for any mixed bit-width of activation and weight. To alleviate the random-access cost of LUT, we propose techniques in both system and algorithm to enable the LUT to reside in the fastest on-chip memory and parallel lookup. On system-side, we propose the <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LUT-centric data layout</span>, to make sure a LUT in on-chip memory i.e., registers, through axis reordering and tiling to fully reuse each table as well as reduce the temporary results which competes with the on-chip memory. On algorithm-side, we propose <span id="S1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">table quantization</span> and <span id="S1.p8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mirror consolidation</span> to reduce the size of tables.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">We implemented T-MAC on the pervasively available CPU processors of edge devices, even a Raspberry Pi. We find T-MAC makes the LLM inference speed on a CPU comparable or even higher to the GPU on the same device, mainly because T-MAC has no conversion cost and the total operation reduction by table lookup. <span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">This paper is thus the first to provide a practical solution for deploying LLMs on edge devices using the widely available CPUs, without relying on GPUs.</span>
We evaluated T-MAC performance on typical edge devices, including Apple M2 Ultra, Jetson AGX Orin, Surface Book 3, and Raspberry Pi 5. The T-MAC kernel speedup can reach up to 6.6<math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and an average of 3.6<math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> compared to the SOTA on the CPU by llama.cpp <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>)</cite>. The e2e LLM inference speedup achieves 2.8<math id="S1.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup for Llama-2-7B-2bit model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite>. The inference performance can reach 11.1 tokens/s even on a Raspberry Pi for BitNet-b1.58-3B model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>)</cite>. T-MAC is also energy efficient, reducing 60-70% energy compared to llama.cpp.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions can be summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">T-MAC transforms the data-type-centric multiplication to <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bit-wise</span> table lookup for a unified and scalable mpGEMM design.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose both system and algorithm techniques to enable the table to reside on the fastest memory and parallel lookup.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement the T-MAC kernel library and e2e inference system to achieve significant LLM inference speedup and energy saving.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/fig_intro.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/166;" width="452" height="166"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">T-MAC vs general practice for mpGEMM.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Background and Motivation</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>LLM on Edge</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized the field of natural language processing, opening new horizons for human-computer interaction and personalized assistant. The deployment of LLMs directly on edge devices, such as smartphones, desktop computers, and robotics, has emerged as a critical frontier in computing, promising to enhance these devices with unprecedented levels of intelligence and autonomy.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-on-edge benefits.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deploying LLMs on edge devices brings several compelling benefits. On-device processing drastically reduces response latencies, which is critical for time-sensitive applications such as autonomous vehicles and interactive robotics. Furthermore, local data processing enhances user privacy by keeping sensitive information confined to the device, thereby reducing the risk of data leakage. Another significant advantage is the operational reliability that comes with network independence, allowing for consistent functionality regardless of network availability or stability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-on-edge challenges.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The primary challenge in deploying LLMs on edge devices is the substantial memory requirement to accomodate these models. LLMs often encompass billions of parameters.
For example, LLAMA-2-7B with FP16 precision requires at least 14GB of memory to host the model. In contrast, edge devices typically have limited memory resources, which poses a stark limitation for on-device deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond memory capacity, the computational and memory bandwidth demands of LLMs present a significant hurdle for edge deployment.
Edge devices often process data in a single-instance fashion, commonly with a batch size of one, to cater to a single user’s real-time interactions.
The inference process of the LLM can be divided into two stages: the prefill and decode.
The prefill stage, with the self-attention mechanism applied across all input tokens, involves compute-intensive matrix-matrix multiplications.
However, once the key-value (KV) cache is generated, the decode stage becomes the bottleneck. In this phase, generating each subsequent token necessitates laoding and processing the entire model, which translates to memory-intensive matrix-vector multiplications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The third challenge is power or energy efficiency, which is particularly critical for battery-operated edge devices such as smartphones and robotics. These devices are designed for prolonged operation on finite energy reserves, making energy efficiency an essential consideration.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Low-Bit (Weight-Quantized) LLM</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The memory-intensive nature of LLM inference necessitates strategies to reduce the model’s memory footprint without significantly compromising model performance. Weight quantization emerges as a key technique to achieve this balance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Weight quantization involves reducing the precision of the model’s parameters, effectively allowing the model to occupy less memory and potentially speed up computation by leveraging lower-precision arithmetic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>)</cite>.
Nowadays, LLMs are increasingly being released with a 4-bit version specifically tailored for deployment on edge or other resource-constrained environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>)</cite>.
Recent research has pushed the boundaries even further, investigating the feasibility of 2-bit and 1-bit weight representations in LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>)</cite>. Fundamentally, the choice of bitwidth or precision in weight quantization represents a trade-off between computational efficiency and model accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3. </span>Deployment Challenges of Low-Bit LLM</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The adoption of low-bit LLMs has become a necessity for edge deployment. In fact, numerous LLM-on-Edge systems and implementations are actively employing low-bit techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>)</cite>.
However, deploying low-bit LLMs introduces unique computational challenges particularly in accommodating mixed-precision operations, which are not natively supported by most hardware architectures, and managing the diversity of bit widths and precision levels required by various deployment scenarios. Addressing these challenges is critical for full potential and seamless intergration of low-bit LLMs in edge computing.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mixed-precison GEMM/GEMV</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The utilization of low-bit (weight-quantized) LLMs introduces a computational paradigm where low precision weights are combined with relatively higher precision activations. This necessitates a shift from standard matrix multiplication operations (i.e., GEMM, GEMV) to mixed-precision ones (i.e., mpGEMM, mpGEMV).
However, current hardware architectures, including CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, do not natively support mixed-precision operations. These architectures are traditionally optimized for standard operations where both operands share the same data type and precision level.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In response to this limitation, existing systems implement an indirect approach by employing dequantization, which involves converting low-precision weights back to a higher precision to align with activation precision. This process enables the use of high-precision GEMM for low-bit LLM inference. For instance, systems like those used in the <span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Intel Neural Compressor</span> and <span id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> rely on this dequantization-based technique. However, the efficacy of such methods is contingent upon the assumption that dequantization does not become a bottleneck and can be overlapped with memory loading. Since this indirect approach ultimately reverts to high-precision computation, it fails to fully capitalize on the benefits of low-bit weights, such as reduced memory usage and potentially faster computation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bit-width/precision diversity</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the challenge of facilitating mixed-precision operations, the diversity of bit-widths and precisions required by different deployment scenarios compounds the complexity. Depending on the task’s difficulty and the specific requirements of the deployment environment, a variety of bit-widths may be selected to optimize performance. No single bit-width or precision setting can universally satisfy the diverse demands of all possible use cases. Consequently, this necessitates computational approaches capable of supporting a spectrum of low-bit widths, ensuring adaptability to the wide-ranging needs of edge computing tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4. </span>LUT-based Computation for Quantized Model</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A new trend in the computation of quantized models is the adoption of Lookup Table (LUT)-based methods.
For quantized Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), where both weights and activations are quantized to levels such as 4-bit, 2-bit, or 1-bit,
DeepGEMM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>)</cite> precomputes all
possible products of weights and activations, stores them in
a lookup table, and efficiently accesses them at inference
time to avoid costly multiply-accumulate operations.
Another example is for vector quantization, where activations are vector quantized, MADDNESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>)</cite> and LUT-NN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>)</cite> also transform GEMM computation to table lookups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the context of low-bit LLMs, or weight-only quantized LLMs, the LUT-based approach has been explored on GPUs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>)</cite>.
These methods leverage the GPU’s shared memory or cache to store and access the lookup tables. However, despite the theoretical reduction in computational complexity, the practical kernel performance is worse than dequantization-based kernels in  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>.
For example, when tested with weight matrix shapes from real-world Llama-2 models on A100 GPU, the average latency of LUT-GEMM kernels  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite> is 2.34<math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, 1.87<math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and 1.75<math id="S2.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer than dequantization-based kernels in BitBLAS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite> for
<math id="S2.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{INT4}}A_{\text{FP16}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>INT4</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mtext>FP16</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{INT4}}A_{\text{FP16}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{INT2}}A_{\text{FP16}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>INT2</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mtext>FP16</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{INT2}}A_{\text{FP16}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{INT1}}A_{\text{FP16}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>INT1</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mtext>FP16</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{INT1}}A_{\text{FP16}}</annotation></semantics></math>
mpGEMVs, respectively.
The suboptimal kernel performance is attributable to the constraints of the GPU’s fixed architecture, which offers either inadequate storage capacity for the lookup tables or insufficiently rapid table access.
In contrast, the exploration of LUT-based mixed-precision GEMM/GEMV on CPUs remains uncharted. Our work pioneers this investigation by examining the viability and performance implications of applying LUT-based methods to CPU-based inference of low-bit LLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Design</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>. </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">T-MAC design overview.</span></figcaption><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/overview.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/272;" width="476" height="272"></object>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Current implementations for mixed-precision GEMM vary case by case. Each bit-width combination of activation and weight, such as W4A16 and W2A8, requires specific weight layout and computing kernels. For example, the layout for W3 could pack 2 bits and the other 1 bit in separate, and leverages different interleaving or swizzling methods for memory alignment or fast decoding. The corresponding computing kernel then needs to unpack this specific layout to a hardware-supported data type for execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To provide a unified and scalable solution for mixed-precision GEMM, this paper transforms the dominant <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">data-type-centric</span> computation to <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bit-wise</span> computation, based on the linear equivalent transformation in Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. For mixed-precision GEMM, <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> are the activation and weight matrix, respectively. <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the bit-width of the weight. <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is each bit matrix of <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\times W=A\times(\sum^{n-1}_{i=0}2^{i}W_{i})=\sum^{n-1}_{i=0}2^{i}A\times W_{i}\vskip-7.22743pt" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\times W=A\times(\sum^{n-1}_{i=0}2^{i}W_{i})=\sum^{n-1}_{i=0}2^{i}A\times W_{i}\vskip-7.22743pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this way, the diverse weight layouts are reduced to a unified one-bit matrix layout. The diverse computing kernels are reduced to unified multiplication of the activation matrix and the one-bit matrix. Besides, bit-wise computation enables the linear scale-down of computation cost with the bit-width reduction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This paper exploits the LUT method to realize this bit-wise layout and multiplication (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), and proposes the LUT-centric data layout (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. LUT-Centric Data Layout ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>), as well as the table compression methods (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. Reduce LUT Storage ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) to enable in-register table residence and the fastest parallel lookup.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>T-MAC Algorithm</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and and Alg. <a href="#algorithm1" title="In Challenges of LUT implementation ‣ 3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the T-MAC design. During the offline preparation stage (line 29 to 35), a <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-bit weight matrix is decomposed into <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> one-bit matrices. Since one bit can only represent two values, for a group with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> bits, the possible permutations are only <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{g}</annotation></semantics></math>. During the online stage, the permutations can be precomputed with each group of activation of shape <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,g]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,g]</annotation></semantics></math> and saved in a table. A <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>-bit group in the weight is thus an index to look up the table for the precomputed results. Therefore, a <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">table</span> in T-MAC is defined to save the results of a <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,g]\times[g,2^{g}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,g]\times[g,2^{g}]</annotation></semantics></math> sub-matrix multiplication, and the table size is <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,2^{g}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,2^{g}]</annotation></semantics></math>. During the offline stage, a tile in the one-bit matrix will be saved continuously in memory to facilitate fast loading. Same as the tiling of normal matrix multiplication, a tiling here is also to improve data locality and cache utilization during LUT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the online stage, given the input activation of a GEMM, T-MAC traverses every <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,g]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,g]</annotation></semantics></math> vector of the activation to multiply with the <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[g,2^{g}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[g,2^{g}]</annotation></semantics></math> bit-pattern matrix and build up a table (line 16 to 27). During LUT, each index (i.e., group) of the one-bit weight matrix is used to look up the tables for partial results (line 6-9). The accumulation of the partial results will be the final GEMM results (line 12-14).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To illustrate with an example, given g=4, for an activation (A1,A2,A3,A4) of shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,4]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,4]</annotation></semantics></math> and 1-bit weights of shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[4,M]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[4,M]</annotation></semantics></math>, the activation will be precomputed online into a LUT of shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,16]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,16]</annotation></semantics></math>, containing elements from -A1-A2-A3-A4 to A1+A2+A3+A4. By grouping every 4 weights together, the weight vector of 0000 will lookup -A1-A2-A3-A4 and 0101 will lookup -A1+A2-A3+A4.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/dataflow.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/406;" width="476" height="406"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Data flow of T-MAC vs general practice.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">An example of LUT-based mpGEMM</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (left) shows an example of the T-MAC materialization on CPU. Taking the group size <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=4</annotation></semantics></math>, the tile size of the index matrix <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}[K_{tk},M_{tm}]=[4,32]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}[K_{tk},M_{tm}]=[4,32]</annotation></semantics></math>, and the bit width as <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=4</annotation></semantics></math>. The right side is the general practice of mpGEMM implementation using llama.cpp. For T-MAC on the left side,
the 32 uint4 indices are first unpacked into uint8 bytes (blue) to ensure compatibility with the hardware data type and instructions. Subsequently, the uint8 indices are utilized to look up the table. The results from the look-up are then split and converted to a higher precision for multiplying with the quantization scales of the low-bit LLM model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">By comparison, the general practice designs specific computing kernels for this 4-bit model. It first directly decodes the 4-bit weight to int8 to align with hardware data type, and then conducts int8 dot-product for the activation and weight vectors. Similarly, the result will be covered into FP16 for multiplying with quantization scales. The cache tiling for llama.cpp is <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W[K_{tk},M_{tm}]=[32,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W[K_{tk},M_{tm}]=[32,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. LUT-Centric Data Layout ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> will explain the different tiling rationale of T-MAC from current practice.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Challenges of LUT implementation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the algorithm and example, it can be seen that LUT-based mpGEMM exposes the following challenges. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i) Random data access.</span> Compared to the continuous data access of current practice, the tables are randomly accessed given the indices. It is necessary to host tables in the fast on-chip memory to reduce the access cost. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii) Enlarged on-chip memory usage.</span> However, LUT requires more on-chip memory compared to current practice. The table size grows exponentially with the group size <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>. For instance, when <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=4</annotation></semantics></math>, the LUT is four times larger than the original activation. Besides, in contrast to the traditional GEMM implementation that yields <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scalar</span> outputs for each basic block, LUT method results in <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vector</span> outputs (as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), which requires more on-chip memory to store the temporary results. Considering the example in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> again, the LUT method uses 144 8-bit registers and llama.cpp uses 104 8-bit registers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address the above issues, we propose two main techniques: (a) <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LUT-centric data layout</span> to accommodate intermediates and LUT into memory with higher bandwidth, and (b) <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reduced LUT storage</span> to decrease the LUT size and limit the number of look-up operations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span>T-MAC GEMM</figcaption>

</div>

</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.3" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">output :</span> Result matrix <math id="algorithm1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="algorithm1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>

<div id="algorithm1.4.9" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6</span></span>
              <span id="algorithm1.4.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.4.9.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="algorithm1.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> 1 to <math id="algorithm1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.4.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.10" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>

<div id="algorithm1.4.28" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.28.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">25</span></span>
              <span id="algorithm1.4.28.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span> <math id="algorithm1.m97" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, …, <math id="algorithm1.m98" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.29" class="ltx_listingline">

</div>
</div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>LUT-Centric Data Layout</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As described in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, the LUT-based method for low-bit GEMM requires more memory to store the lookup table and the intermediate results.
On the other hand, the table look-ups usually lead to memory access inefficiency due to the random memory accesses.
To resolve the inefficiency on memory storage and accesses, we design a LUT-centric data layout for the LUT-based low-bit GEMM. Specifically, it stores the lookup table on on-chip memory like registers to accelerate table accesses, and designs axis reordering and data tiling to enhance data reuses for reducing memory consumption.
Furthermore, to improve the efficiency, we design two data layout optimizations, i.e., weight permutation to align with memory transactions, and weight interleaving for optimizing weight unpack.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Put lookup table on on-chip memory.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The LUT-based GEMM described in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> requires fetching the result from the pre-computed table, which should access the lookup table randomly. To accelerate these table look-ups, we put the lookup table on registers, and leverage the hardware-specific instructions (e.g., TBL on ARM CPUs and PSHUF on x86 CPUs) to do table look-ups. The details of optimizing table look-ups with hardware-specific instructions will be described in §<a href="#S4" title="4. Implementation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
However, putting the lookup table on registers further increases the memory pressure on the on-chip memory, which may result in dramatic performance drop due to memory spilling. To fully explore the potential of on-chip memory table look-ups, we design axis reordering and tiling to enhance data reuses to reduce the on-chip memory pressure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Axis reordering.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For GEMM <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[N,M]=A[N,K]\times W[M,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[N,M]=A[N,K]\times W[M,K]</annotation></semantics></math>, it is natural to loop among the spatial axes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, and then the temporal axis <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>. However, the LUT-based GEMM needs to build the table among the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> axis, resulting in extreme large table storage when looping spatial axes then temporal axis following the traditional GEMM, i.e., a lookup table for the whole <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A[N,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A[N,K]</annotation></semantics></math>
But if we swap the axis order from spatial first to temporal first, it will only maintain a small lookup table <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,K]</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, T-MAC reorders the axes access to temporal axis <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> first and then spatial axes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tiling.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tiling is a common technique in optimizing data locality of GEMM and reducing the memory requirements by reusing data on on-chip memory. Assume the GEMM <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[N,M]=A[N,K]\times W[M,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[N,M]=A[N,K]\times W[M,K]</annotation></semantics></math> is processed with tile <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A[N_{tn},K_{tk}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A[N_{tn},K_{tk}]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W[M_{tm},K_{tk}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W[M_{tm},K_{tk}]</annotation></semantics></math>, processing a tile requires <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{tn}*K_{tk}+M_{tm}*K_{tk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{tn}*K_{tk}+M_{tm}*K_{tk}</annotation></semantics></math> data loading from DRAM to processor’s on-chip memory instead of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{tn}*M_{tm}*K_{tk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{tn}*M_{tm}*K_{tk}</annotation></semantics></math> data loading. In traditional GEMM, the tile size <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{tn}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{tn}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{tm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{tm}</annotation></semantics></math> have equal effects on efficiency while <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{tk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{tk}</annotation></semantics></math> does not affect the data reusing and is set to align the memory transaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, in LUT-based GEMM, the activation <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A[N,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A[N,K]</annotation></semantics></math> should be processed to build the lookup table, while the weight <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W[M,K]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W[M,K]</annotation></semantics></math> can share the same pre-computed lookup table. That is to say, a larger tile size <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{tm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{tm}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> can lead to better lookup table reusing. T-MAC will carefully consider the tiling configurations <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{tn}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{tn}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{tm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{tm}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{tk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{tk}</annotation></semantics></math> to achieve better data reusing.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/interleaving.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/160;" width="452" height="160"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Interleave weights for fast unpacking.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layout optimizations.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond optimizing the on-chip table lookups with axis reordering and tiling, we design two data layout optimizations, i.e., weight permutation and interleaving, to further improve the efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weight permutation for sequential memory access.  </span>
DRAM requires sequential accesses to achieve higher bandwidth utilization, while accessing tiles in the tiling-based GEMM introduces random accesses because tiles of the input matrices are not sequentially stored.
To solve this problem, T-MAC designs a weight permutation method that permutes the weight matrix to align the weight load with the memory transaction.
After the scheduling of a GEMM is determined, T-MAC will permute the input matrices to let tiles stored sequentially instead of the whole matrices. Specifically, T-MAC flats the elements in a tile sequentially and then concatenates the flatten tiles according to the tile accessing order.
Note that the weight matrix will not be modified during LLM inference, so this permutation can be done in offline. This offline permutation does not introduce cost in inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weight interleaving for fast unpacking.  </span>
As described in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, the weight matrix is stored in packed format in memory and should be unpacked during computation.
However, due to the commonly-used little-endian in modern CPUs, bytes in an integer are stored in a backward order. Therefore, using the integer instructions to unpack the weights requires additional reordering to return the correct unpacked weights.
As the weight matrix will not be modified during LLM inference, T-MAC can interleave the packed weights to eliminate this reordering. Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Tiling. ‣ 3.2. LUT-Centric Data Layout ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows an example of this interleaving that unpacking the interleaved weights can directly produce the required weights sequentially.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Reduce LUT Storage</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the realm of LUT-based method for low-bit LLM inference, the size of the lookup table is a crucial factor that impacts both the storage requirements and the access latency, especially when optimizing table look-ups with on-chip memory in §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. LUT-Centric Data Layout ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.
A larger table size not only demands more memory space, but also leads to slower table access speed.
To address this challenge, we introduce two optimization strategies: <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mirror consolidation</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">table quantization</span>.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3. Reduce LUT Storage ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, mirror consolidation exploits the symmetrical properties of table values to halve the length of the table, while table quantization applies quantization techniques to the table values themselves to reduce the width of the table. Combined, these methods enable a significant reduction in the storage footprint of the lookup table (up to a quarter of its original size) without accuracy loss in the LLM inference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/table_reduction.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/209;" width="476" height="209"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Reduce LUT storage with mirror consolidation and table quantization. Mirror consolidation halves the table length. Table quantization reduces the table width.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mirror Consolidation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The inherent symmetrical properties of table values in the context of lookup tables for LLM inference present a unique opportunity for optimization. Each positive value within the table is naturally paired with its negative counterpart, reflecting a mirror image across the zero value. Leveraging this symmetry, our proposed <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Mirror Consolidation</span> technique capitalizes on the fact that only half of the table values need to be explicitly stored. The remaining half can be rapidly reconstructed by simply negating the stored values. This table compression method is lossless, preserving the model’s inference accuracy entirely. Furthermore, it proves to be highly efficient, accelerating the precomputation of the lookup table, reducing the required storage, and speeding up table accesses.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Table Quantization.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table quantization operates on a principle analogous to weight and activation quantization, aiming to reduce the precision of table values for improved computational efficiency. For instance, values initially represented in 16-bit floating-point (fp16) within a lookup table can be quantized to 8-bit integer (int8) with a scaling factor.
The impact of table quantization on model accuracy is negligible. Contrary to activation quantization, which has been challenging in maintaining model accuracy due to its necessity for coarse granularity and static quantization to ensure fast computation, our approach embraces finer granularity (quantizing 8 values for k=4) and dynamic quantization to minimize accuracy degradation. The findings presented in §<a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6. Error Analysis ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a> demonstrate that our table quantization technique has an imperceptible effect on the overall model accuracy.
In terms of efficiency, table quantization significantly reduces lookup table storage requirements and accelerates the lookup process.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Implementation</h2>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
