<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Code generation through TVM</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ TVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>)</cite> + LLVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>)</cite> for code generation. This allows us to generate optimal code for GEMM of varying shapes and for different hardware, and implement common optimizations such as loop unrolling, vectorization, and constant folding. We utilize TVM Tensorize to embed hardware intrinsics into the code. AutoTVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>)</cite> is used to automatically fine-tune the generated code for different hardware targets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">API and integration</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a consistent API for both C++ and Python. The GEMM functions are encapsulated into TVM PackedFunc, and the tensors can be transferred through the DLPack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>)</cite> tensor structure. This facilitates easy interoperability with other frameworks like PyTorch, Numpy, and etc. Additionally, we provide an additional wrapper for C++, where tensors can be passed through raw pointers and TVM runtime dependency is eliminated. This offers a more lightweight solution for integration into other C++ projects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parallelism</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize the TVM runtime threadpool to dynamically assign tasks to CPUs. However, when integrating T-MAC into llama.cpp, we notice an obvious conflict between the llama.cpp threadpool and the TVM threadpool. This conflict arises as threads from different threadpools compete for CPU resources, leading to a significant performance degradation. To resolve this issue, we generate C++ code using TVM, rather than directly creating library files, and then postprocess the code to remove the dependency on the TVM runtime and threadpool. The generated function will only execute computations of a single threadblock, and then we assign these threadblocks to different threads in the llama.cpp threadpool. This approach achieves better performance and compatibility with llama.cpp. The portable C++ code also offers an option for cross-platform deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiant table look-up by TBL/PSHUF</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After loading the table into registers, we can utilize hardware intrinsics provided by ARM NEON/INTEL AVX2. Both NEON/AVX2 offer 8-bit look-up instructions. The bit width of ARM NEON is 128, which can precisely accommodate the entire table of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=4</annotation></semantics></math>. INTEL AVX2 has a bit width of 256, but the lower and upper halves are in separate 128-bit lanes. Therefore, we duplicate the table to fill the 256-bit LUT register and look up 32 different int8 weight indices with a single instruction. If the table’s data type is float16, since NEON/AVX2 do not support 16-bit LUT, we split float16 into two 8-bit LUTs, one for the lower part and the other for the higher part. We can look up the lower and higher parts with two instructions and then recombine them into float16.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Determine the size of on-chip LUT</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The number of on-chip LUTs is tuned for each hardware, to make sure on-chip memory can be fully utilized and LUTs won’t be swapped out for the tile. Larger on-chip memory allows more LUTs to reside, enabling more intermediate results to be aggregated before writing back. Register spill caused by excessive on-chip LUTs can lead to overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is also determined by the on-chip memory size and instruction throughput. LUT for <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=4</annotation></semantics></math> exactly fits into one register for ARM.TBL/AVX2.PSHUF. A larger <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, such as <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=5</annotation></semantics></math>, requires two registers and slower ARM.TBL2/AVX512.PSHUF.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fast 8-bit aggregation</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Besides table look-up, aggregation is another significant computational overhead. To speed up the aggregation, we initially aggregate the look-up results in low bit and later convert the aggregation sum to a higher precision like float16 with no accuracy loss. Moreover, we can implement fast 8-bit aggregation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>)</cite> if the table is quantized to int8. Normally, the int8 values should be converted to int16 to avoid overflow. However, int16 instructions have half the throughput of int8 aggregation. As an alternative, we can use <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">avg/rhadd</span> instructions to compute the average and minimize accuracy loss by subtracting the probabilistic bias from the final value. Notably, fast 8-bit aggregation could result in nonnegligible accuracy loss.
In Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4. Implementation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we list the hardware intrinsics for look-up and aggregation on different CPU architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bit-serial linear transformation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the decomposition mentioned in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we utilize the original values of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., 0 and 1. However, we can introduce a linear transformation to these values. Denote this linear transformation as <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(v_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(v_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and the transformed values as <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(0)=s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(0)=s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(1)=s_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(1)=s_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To speed up precomputation and reduce quantization error, the values of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> need to be chosen with care. To circumvent float-multiply instructions, we select them from the set [-1, 0, 1]. To reduce quantization error, we strive to minimize the difference between the largest and smallest entries of the lookup table (LUT). From empirical studies, we have found that <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}=-1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{1}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1}=1</annotation></semantics></math> are optimal choices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By setting the values of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the linear transformation <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and the decomposition of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> should be adjusted as follows:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}^{\prime}v_{i}+\beta_{i}^{\prime},v_{i}=\alpha_{i}f(v_{i})+\beta_{i}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}^{\prime}v_{i}+\beta_{i}^{\prime},v_{i}=\alpha_{i}f(v_{i})+\beta_{i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Register swizzling for efficient LUT precomputation</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As demonstrated in §<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. T-MAC Algorithm ‣ 3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we opt for subtraction/addition instructions over multiplication instructions to achieve better throughput. For the LUT of shape <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(N,K/g,2^{g})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(N,K/g,2^{g})</annotation></semantics></math>, the subtraction/addition can be vectorized along the <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K/g</annotation></semantics></math> axis. For instance,</p>
<table id="S4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle LUT[0,0:8,0]=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>U</mi><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle LUT[0,0:8,0]=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle-A[0,0:32:4]-A[0,1:32:4]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle-A[0,0:32:4]-A[0,1:32:4]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle-A[0,2:32:4]-A[0,3:32:4]\vskip-3.61371pt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle-A[0,2:32:4]-A[0,3:32:4]\vskip-3.61371pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The indexing into <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is not contiguous. By employing <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LD4</span> in NEON and <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vgatherdps</span> in AVX2, we can efficiently load non-contiguous data. However, when writing the non-contiguous LUT back into memory, extracting specific bytes from a SIMD register and writing to memory is highly inefficient for AVX2. To address this issue, we use register swizzling to rearrange the LUT so that it can be written back to memory contiguously. Initially, we use <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vpblendvb</span> to blend 8-bit values from different registers into one register, followed by <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vpermd</span> to swizzle the 32-bit values of the 256-bit, and then <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vpshufb</span> to further shuffle the 8-bit values into the correct order. After swizzling, the LUT can be written back to memory in a contiguous manner.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>. </span><span id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Hardware device specification.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate T-MAC with real-world, low-bit LLMs, specifically Llama and BitNet, across four distinct edge devices. Our benchmarking efforts are aimed at a direct comparison with the existing state-of-the-art <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> implementation. We summarize our key findings as follows:</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The mpGEMV and mpGEMM kernels of T-MAC show a marked performance gain, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art dequantization-based kernels.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">T-MAC enables an end-to-end model inference throughput improvement of 2-4x, while concurrently reducing the energy consumption by 60%-70% relative to the original <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> implementation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Remarkably, in many cases, T-MAC not only matches but even exceeds GPU performance, indicating a new milestone for LLM deployment efficiency on devices.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1. </span>Evaluation Setup</h3>

<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>. </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">mpGEMV performance benchmark at 1/2/3/4 bits with single-thread and multi-thread. Matrix shapes are from Llama-2-7b and Llama-2-13b. The 1-bit kernel performance of llama.cpp is deduced from its 2-bit kernel and marked with dashed lines.</span></figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hardware devices</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we evaluate T-MAC across four distinct edge devices. These devices range from high-performance ones like M2-Ultra to less powerful ones like Raspberry Pi. The CPUs tested encompass Intel Core, Apple Silicon, and Cortex series. The operating systems include OSX, Linux, and Windows. This evaluation guarantees T-MAC’s cross-platform compatibility and consistent performance across different instruction sets and various edge deployment scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Kernels and models</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the performance of T-MAC, we conduct extensive benchmarks using real-word low-bit LLMs and scenarios.
For the kernel performance benchmark, we select matrix shapes derived from the Llama-2-7B and Llama-2-13B models, ensuring our evaluation reflects the practical demands.
To conduct an end-to-end throughput test, we employed actual quantized models to demonstrate the practical efficacy of T-MAC across different bit-width configurations.
Specifically, we employ 4-bit,3-bit,2-bit and 1-bit quantized Llama models, and also 1-bit and 1.58bit BitNet models that are trained from scratch. Ternary weights in 1.58bit BitNet are interpreted as 2-bit and decomposed into two 1-bit matrices.
The 4-bit Llama models are from GPTQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>)</cite>.
The 3-bit and 2-bit Llama models are from BitDistiller <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>)</cite>.
The 1-bit Llama models are from OneBit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compared the performance of T-MAC with <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> (version b2794, realesed on May 2024), a state-of-the-art implementation for LLM deployment on edge devices.
We chose <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> as the baseline for several compelling reasons. Firstly, <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> represents the cutting-edge in LLM deployment on edge devices, featuring highly optimized kernel implementations tailored to each hardware platform. Its versatility and robust performance make it an ideal benchmark for assessing the efficacy of new methodologies. Additionally, <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> is implemented in plain C/C++ without any dependencies, ensuring maximum compatibility and efficiency across diverse hardware configurations. For kernel performance benchmarks, we utilized the optimized kernels provided by <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> as the baselines on the respective hardware devices. In our end-to-end throughput evaluations, we integrate the LUT-based kernels from T-MAC to <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> and compare it with original <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also compared the performance of T-MAC with <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp (BLAS)</span>. <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> uses <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Accelerate</span> on M2-Ultra and <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">OpenBLAS</span> on the other platforms. <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp (BLAS)</span> is slower for mpGEMV but faster for mpGEMM compared to <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span>’s highly optimized mixed-precision implementation. Therefore, T-MAC is measured against <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">BLAS</span> only for mpGEMM.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Measurement approach.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform both <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">kernel-level</span> and <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">model-level</span> measurement. To obtain precise and consistent kernel-level latency on CPU, we first perform a warmup of 10 iterations, followed by 100 runs to calculate an average. The warmup on M2-Ultra differs slightly from the others, requiring at least 1 second to maximize performance. To perform model-level latency, we integrate T-MAC into llama.cpp. We repeatedly generate 64 tokens for 20 iterations to evaluate token generation throughput.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>. </span><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">mpGEMM performance benchmark at 1/2/3/4 bits with multi-thread. Matrix shapes are from Llama-2-7b and Llama-2-13b with an input sequence length of 256. The 1-bit kernel performance of llama.cpp is deduced from its 2-bit kernel and marked with dashed lines.</span></figcaption><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/gemm.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/138;" width="476" height="138"></object>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2. </span>mpGEMV/mpGEMM Performance Benchmark</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the kernels in Llama-2-7B/13B across all four devices. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.1. Evaluation Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> with the bits decrease from 4-bit to 2-bit, llama.cpp fails to gain any additional speedup, and even experiences a 15% slowdown at 3-bit compared to 4-bit due to decoding overhead. Therefore, we can infer that the 1-bit llama.cpp performance would be similar to 2-bit, even though llama.cpp does not provide a 1-bit implementation. In contrast, T-MAC achieves linear speedup with bit reduction. For single-threaded GEMV, T-MAC achieves maximum speedups of 11.2x, 5.8x, 4.7x, and 3.1x respectively for 1/2/3/4 bits.
For multi-threaded mpGEMV, T-MAC’s performance is primarily constrained by memory bandwidth, but T-MAC can still achieve significant speedup due to efficient memory access. For example, with 2-bit, T-MAC achieves 4.0x, 4.0x, 5.31 and 2.5x on all four devices respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate mpGEMM with a sequence length of 256 for multi-threading in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Measurement approach. ‣ 5.1. Evaluation Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> uses BLAS for mpGEMM. T-MAC still achieves significant speedup on RBP, Orin, and Surface for 2-bit with maximum speedups of 4.0x, 5.3x, and 5.3x respectively. M2-Ultra is an exception, as the Apple Silicon CPUs are equipped with a powerful AMX coprocessor to handle GEMM operations. However, T-MAC still achieves a maximum 2.0<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup for 1-bit in this case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">T-MAC demonstrates a significant advantage at 3-bit precision. This can be attributed to the inefficiencies in current techniques for handling 3-bit weights. Weights decoding is typically executed using SHIFT and AND instructions, which require weights being aligned with the width of bytes. Since 8 is indivisible by 3, this decoding process is notably inefficient. <span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> attempts to optimize it by separately packing 2 bits and the remaining 1 bit, but it still results in significant overhead. In contrast, T-MAC avoids this problem by individually computing the results of each bit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3. </span>End-to-End Inference Throughput</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After integrating into llama.cpp, we compare the end-to-end token generation throughput of llama.cpp with T-MAC. We employ 2-bit to execute BitNet. As depicted in Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5.3. End-to-End Inference Throughput ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, under single-threading on Raspberry Pi 5, T-MAC achieves speedups of 2.8x, 6.7x, and 5.8x for the three models respectively. Under multi-threading, due to memory constraints and operators other than mpGEMV/mpGEMM, the speedup is less pronounced. However, we still observe speedups of 1.1x, 2.3x, and 1.7x on M2-Ultra.
T-MAC can reach a peak of 71 tokens/sec on the powerful M2-Ultra and 11 tokens/sec on the less powerful Raspberry Pi 5, indicating promising real-world edge deployment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/e2e.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/381;" width="476" height="381"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>. </span><span id="S5.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">End-to-end token generation throughput by integrating T-MAC kernels into llama.cpp. M1, M2 and M3 stands for Llama-2-7B-4bit, Llama-2-7B-2bit and BitNet-3B.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4. </span>Power and Energy Consumption</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to computational efficiency, energy efficiency is equally critical, especially for edge devices that rely on battery power.
To evaluate the power and energy consumption of T-MAC relative to <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span>, we conducted experiments using multi-threaded implementations on the M2 Ultra device. We selected three models for our analysis: Llama-2-7B-4bit, Llama-2-7B-2bit, and BitNet-3B.
The power usage is measured using <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">powermetrics</span> on OSX, which can record the average power usage over a specified sample interval. We set this interval to 500 milliseconds, continuously generate tokens for a minimum of 120 seconds, and compute the integral of power over time to determine the total energy consumption.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S5.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 5.4. Power and Energy Consumption ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, indicate a significant reduction in power consumption when using the LUT-based kernels in T-MAC.
For the models Llama-2-7B-4bit, Llama-2-7B-2bit, and BitNet-3B, T-MAC demonstrates a power consumption reduction of 10.3%, 10.3%, and 17.3%, respectively. These reductions in power consumption, combined with the latency gains offered by T-MAC, lead to a substantial decrease in total energy consumption. Specifically, T-MAC reduces energy consumption by 20.6%, 61.2%, and 51.3% for each model, respectively.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/e2e_power.svg" id="S5.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/240;" width="476" height="240"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>. </span><span id="S5.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Power and energy consumption for multi-threaded inference on M2-Ultra. M1, M2 and M3 stands for Llama-2-7B-4bit, Llama-2-7B-2bit and BitNet-3B respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5. </span>Optimization Breakdown</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the effectiveness of the optimizations in §<a href="#S3" title="3. Design ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we break down our optimization strategies. Most of these optimizations yield greater benefits for single-threading, but tiling requires multi-threading to be effective, hence this evaluation is conducted using multi-threading. While most optimizations are orthogonal, some are dependent on others, for instance, the permutation requires tiling to be completed first. Consequently, we begin with a basic implementation, <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">TM-base</span>, and progressively apply optimizations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">TM-base</span> version utilizes hardware intrinsics to speed up table lookup, but does not implement any memory access optimization. As depicted in Figure <a href="#S5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 5.5. Optimization Breakdown ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, its performance is at most 17% slower compared to the llama.cpp baseline. After implementing <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">table quantization</span>, the performance becomes competitive with llama.cpp. The <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tiling</span> optimization further yields a maximum speedup of 1.45x. By rearranging the data layout into contiguous memory for each tiling, <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">permutation</span> contributes an additional 1.39x speedup. <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Tuning</span> does not appear to be very effective in the figure, as the default tiling configurations already align well with M2-Ultra registers and caches, but for different devices, tuning should assist in finding a better configuration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Upon applying <span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weights interleaving</span>, we obtain T-MAC. Interleaving eliminates most of the unpacking overhead, achieving a 1.42x speedup. The aggressive <span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span> can make T-MAC up to 1.29x faster, but it could lead to non-negligible accuracy loss, so we offer it as an optional optimization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/ablation.svg" id="S5.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/210;" width="476" height="210"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>. </span><span id="S5.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Multi-threaded performance of Llama-2-7B/13B GEMV kernels on M2-Ultra by applying T-MAC optimizations step-by-step. S0-S5: different shapes as shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.1. Evaluation Setup ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. TM: T-MAC, TQ: Table Quantization, Perm.: Permutation, IL: Interleaving, FA: Fast Aggregation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6. </span>Error Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">There are two sources of error compared to conventional mpGEMM implementation: (a) <span id="S5.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">table quantization</span>, which is an algorithmic approximation included in our method, and (b) <span id="S5.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span>, whose error is introduced during the instruction execution within the fixed CPU architecture. We evaluate the impact of these two error sources at both kernel-level and model-level.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Kernel-level Evaluation.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the unquantized
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{FP16}A_{FP16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{FP16}A_{FP16}</annotation></semantics></math> GEMV as the benchmark. The weights and activation of the GEMV are randomly generated FP16 values following a <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Gaussian Distribution</span>, which are then quantized to 4-bit for execution by llama.cpp and T-MAC. The Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) is then computed between the ground truth and the mpGEMV outputs. As shown in Table. <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Kernel-level Evaluation. ‣ 5.6. Error Analysis ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the NMSE difference between llama.cpp and T-MAC is negligible, indicating that the table quantization error is minimal. However, after applying <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span>, the NMSE increases to 2.5<math id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T3.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>. </span><span id="S5.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">End-to-end throughput and model quality of Llama-2-7B-4bit on M2-Ultra with single-thread. T-MAC improves throughput by 1.3<math id="S5.T4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> compared to llama.cpp with the same model quality. Fast Aggregation (FA) can further improve the throughput gain to 1.6<math id="S5.T4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, but the model quality will drop because of the numerical error of current CPU instructions.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model-level Evaluation.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine the impact of these errors on real-world models, we chose Llama-2-7B for testing. The models are the GGUF model converted from official Llama-2-7B weights for the un-quantized ground truth and the original llama-2-7b.Q4_0.gguf model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite> released with llama.cpp for mpGEMM. After integrating T-MAC into llama.cpp, we conduct the evaluation through the <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">perplexity</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>)</cite> tool provided by llama.cpp. The evaluation is performed on three different tasks: <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">WikiText-2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>)</cite> and <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">lambada_openai</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>)</cite> for perplexity (the lower the better), and <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">WinoGrande</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>)</cite> for question answering accuracy (the higher the better. As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Kernel-level Evaluation. ‣ 5.6. Error Analysis ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, on all of the three tasks, T-MAC delivers the same results compared to llama.cpp, suggesting that the error introduced by T-MAC is negligible for real-world models. After toggling on the <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span>, the perplexity increases by 0.4 and 1.0 respectively and the accuracy drops by 0.3%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, T-MAC introduces negligible error to model inference while offering significant speedup. The <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span> can further enhance performance, but at the cost of model quality. We offer this as an option for users in scenarios that prioritize real-time performance and are less sensitive to accuracy. Without <span id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fast aggregation</span>, T-MAC can still achieve substantial gain according to Figure <a href="#S5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 5.5. Optimization Breakdown ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. In the future, we anticipate the error introduced by fast aggregation can be mitigated with straightforward optimizations of the CPU micro-architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.7. </span>Compared with GPU/NPU</h3>

<div id="S5.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPUs are widely used in LLM deployments. We compare T-MAC on CPU with llama.cpp on GPU to illustrate the efficiency of T-MAC.
llama.cpp is the state-of-the-art LLM inference framework for both CPU and GPU on edge devices.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F11" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2407.00088v2/gemv_cuda.svg" id="S5.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/158;" width="476" height="158"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F11.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>. </span><span id="S5.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">mpGEMV kernels performance of T-MAC (CPU) and llama.cpp (GPU) on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.7. Compared with GPU/NPU ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the mpGEMV kernel performance comparsion of T-MAC (CPU) and llama.cpp (GPU) on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, a platform with ARM CPU and NVIDIA CUDA GPU. The kernel configurations are all from Llama-2-7B. T-MAC significantly outperforms GPU on W1A16 on all cases, while achieves comparable performance on W2A16 and W3A16. Although GPU performs better on higher bits and larger shape due to its powerful parallel computing capacity, this evaluation still shows huge potential of CPU-based LLM deployments on edge devices.</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T7.3.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">8.24</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">1.60</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T7.3.4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">11.30</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T7.3.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T7.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">Llama-2-7B-2bit</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.T7.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16.62</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">6.95</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">1.72</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">11.30*</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T7.3.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T7.3.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" rowspan="2"><span id="S5.T7.3.6.1.1" class="ltx_text">Jetson Orin NX</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">Llama-2-7B-4bit</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">7.53</td>

<td id="S5.T7.3.6.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T7.3.6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">14.76</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" rowspan="2"><span id="S5.T7.3.6.6.1" class="ltx_text">-</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T7.3.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T7.3.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">Llama-2-7B-2bit</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S5.T7.3.7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">11.41</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">3.20</td>
<td id="S5.T7.3.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">7.94</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>. </span><span id="S5.T7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Token generation tokens/s of T-MAC vs GPU/NPU for Llama-2-7B-4bit/2bit on three devices. The 2-bit performance of NPUs is deduced from 4-bit and marked with "*".</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.7. Compared with GPU/NPU ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the end-to-end comparison of the Llama-2-7B-2bit model on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Without T-MAC, CPU only performs better than GPU in power, however, the energy consumption is still worse than GPU due to lower throughput. Compared to llama.cpp on CPU, T-MAC not only improves the throughput to 2.2<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, but also reduces the power to 69<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>%</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%</annotation></semantics></math>, resulting in 3.2<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> energy efficiency. Compared to llama.cpp on GPU, although T-MAC only achieves 78<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>%</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%</annotation></semantics></math> throughput, T-MAC only needs 34<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>%</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%</annotation></semantics></math> power, resulting in 2.3<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> energy efficiency. Note that Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.7. Compared with GPU/NPU ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows T-MAC outperforms the GPU on the mpGEMV kernels. The reason why the throughput of T-MAC is still lower than that of GPU is due to the performance of kernels except mpGEMVs in llama.cpp on CPU.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to its power efficiency, T-MAC also demonstrates superior performance over GPU/NPUs across widely used platforms. We further evaluate T-MAC on three devices: Surface Laptop 7, OnePlus 12 and Jetson Orin NX. The full specifications of equipped CPU/GPU/NPUs are detailed in Table <a href="#S5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 5.7. Compared with GPU/NPU ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. We utilize the minimum number of CPU cores that can fully leverage the memory bandwidth and nearly achieve optimal performance. GPU evaluations use the llama.cpp CUDA backend for the NVIDIA GPU and OpenCL backend for the Qualcomm GPU. The performance of NPUs are sourced from official data released by Qualcomm via Qualcomm AI Hub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With T-MAC, CPUs can achieve much higher computation throughput and fully exploit the memory bandwidth. GPU/NPUs, which are also memory-bound for GEMV during token generation, share unified memory with CPUs on most edge devices. As demonstrated in Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 5.7. Compared with GPU/NPU ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ T-MAC: CPU Renaissance via Table Lookup for Low-Bit LLM Deployment on Edge" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, T-MAC achieves significant speedup for Llama-2-7B-2bit on all three devices. Specifically, T-MAC achieves 3<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup on Surface Laptop 7 over the NPU with only 4 out of the total 12 CPU cores, 1.5<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over the NPU on OnePlus 12, and 1.4<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over the Ampere GPU on the Jetson Orin NX. Even for Llama-2-7B-4bit, T-MAC maintains 2.1<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup on Surface Laptop 7. Notably, on OnePlus 12, T-MAC demonstrates a substantial speedup of 6.4<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and 9.7<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> over the Adreno GPU for 4-bit and 2-bit respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, T-MAC, leveraging widely available CPUs, delivers a notable performance advantage over GPUs, and even NPUs specially designed for AI workloads. This makes T-MAC a practical solution for LLM deployment on edge devices.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM Quantization Algorithm</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM quantization has emerged as a crucial technique for the efficient deployment of LLMs in resource-constrained environments.
A segment of the research has been dedicated to the dual quantization of both weights and activations.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LLM.int8()</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>)</cite> isolates outlier feature dimensions to 16-bit computations while processing majority dimensions in efficient 8-bit computations.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SmoothQuant</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>)</cite> migrates the quantization difficulty from activations to weights with a mathematically equivalent transformation to enable an INT8 quantization of both weights and activations.
Advancements in the field have led to a refined focus on the singular quantization of model weights, as weight storage accounts for the majority of memory footprint.
Specific algorithms such as <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">GPTQ</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>)</cite> and <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">AWQ</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>)</cite> have demonstrated the feasibility of quantizing LLMs to just 4 bits using post-training quantization techniques.
Furthermore, <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">BitDistiller</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>)</cite> pushes the boundary to 2 bits by leveraging quantization-aware training (QAT) and self-distillation.
Meanwhile, <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">BitNet</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>)</cite> takes an even more ambitious route by training 1-bit LLMs from scratch.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM Inference System</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The significance of LLMs has spurred the development of various LLM inference systems, tailored to different platforms and optimized for specific goals.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vLLM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>)</cite> is a high-throughput and memory-efficient inference engine designed for LLMs, which excels in large batch processing.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">llama.cpp</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>)</cite> stands out with its plain C/C++ implementation, free of external dependencies, which delivers superior performance on edge computing devices.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">TensorRT-LLM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>)</cite> incorporates a suite of state-of-the-art optimizations specifically for NVIDIA GPUs.
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Intel Neural Compressor</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>)</cite> provides an open-source Python library for model compression techniques, tailored to enhance the efficiency of LLMs within the Intel ecosystem.
All of these inference systems share a crucial capability for supporting low-bit LLMs, which not only minimizes memory usage but also enhances computational efficiency, thereby broadening the accessibility of LLMs for diverse applications.
To complement the landscape of end-to-end LLM inference systems, there are also efforts concentrated on developing highly efficient computational kernels tailored for low-bit LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7. </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">T-MAC transforms the data-type-centric multiplication to bit-wise table lookup, and provide a unified and scalable solution for the increasingly popular mpGEMM. On the pervasively available CPUs of edge devices, T-MAC kernels achieve up to 6.6<math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup compared to llama.cpp, which makes the CPU inference speed comparable or even higher than the GPU on the same device. T-MAC thus provides a practical solution to deploy LLMs on edge devices without relying on GPU, even on a Raspberry Pi. T-MAC also opens up the broad opportunity for novel LLM hardware accelerator design based on LUT, as LUT is much more efficient in hardware implementation than multiplications.</p>
</div>
</section>
